name: City of Madison

actions.title: 12-Month Moratorium on New Data Center Zoning Approvals
actions.summary: The Madison Common Council voted to block zoning approvals for new data centers larger than 10,000 sq ft for up to one year while the city develops a formal land-use definition and zoning standards.

contextBlurb: Madison's zoning code lacked any definition of 'data centers,' historically treating them under an outdated 'telecommunications centers' category. The Common Council enacted a 12-month moratorium on January 13, 2026, to give city staff time to consult other municipalities, review research, and draft appropriate land-use standards. The city also participates in the Dane County Advisory Committee on Data Centers (ACDC) to share findings.

name: Dane County

actions.title: 18-Month Moratorium on Hyperscale Data Center Zoning Permits (RES-039)
actions.summary: Dane County enacted an 18-month moratorium halting receipt of applications and issuance of zoning permits for data centers in towns under county zoning authority, while the Advisory Committee on Data Centers completes its policy research.

contextBlurb: Dane County introduced resolution 2026 RES-039 on May 15, 2026, citing that data center development was inconsistent with the county's Comprehensive Plan and zoning ordinances. The moratorium applies only to towns under county zoning and does not affect cities, villages, or towns with their own codes. County Board Chair Patrick Miles encouraged those other jurisdictions to adopt their own moratoriums to benefit from the Advisory Committee's work.

name: Manitowoc County

actions.title: 18-Month Moratorium on Data Center Permitting
actions.summary: The Manitowoc County Board unanimously approved an 18-month moratorium prohibiting the county from accepting applications or issuing permits for construction or siting of data centers, triggered by concerns from three northeastern Wisconsin towns.

contextBlurb: The towns of Two Creeks, Two Rivers, and Mishicot petitioned Manitowoc County in February 2026 after a data center developer approached landowners in the area. The county's Planning and Park Commission approved a moratorium measure in March before the full board enacted it unanimously on April 29, 2026. The moratorium specifically targets facilities capable of managing more than one petabyte of data and was carefully worded to avoid violating Wisconsin statutes that bar counties from enacting development moratoriums.

name: Town of Cassville (Grant County)

actions.title: Two-Year Data Center Ban Ordinance
actions.summary: Town electors unanimously authorized the Cassville Town Board to exercise zoning authority and pass an ordinance banning data centers for two years across the town's 36 square miles bordering the Mississippi River.

contextBlurb: Residents of Cassville mobilized in spring 2026 after learning the town was on a shortlist for a proposed $1 billion, 400–500 MW data center campus whose developer and location were kept secret under nondisclosure arrangements. With the backing of the 'No Data Centers in the Driftless' opposition network, town electors voted 44–0 to authorize new zoning authority and immediately ban data centers for two years. Grant County cannot preempt the town's newly established local zoning authority.

name: City of Port Washington (Ozaukee County)

actions.title: Voter Referendum Requiring Approval for Large TIF Districts
actions.summary: Port Washington voters approved a referendum (66% in favor) requiring voter approval before the city can create Tax Incremental Financing districts of $10 million or more, directly limiting the city's ability to provide tax incentives to future data center projects without public consent.

contextBlurb: Port Washington is already home to a $15 billion OpenAI/Oracle/Vantage 'Lighthouse' data center campus that broke ground in December 2024, supported by a $458 million TIF district approved without a public vote. Community group Great Lakes Neighbors United collected over 1,000 signatures to force the referendum onto the April 7, 2026 spring ballot, where it passed 66–34%. The measure does not affect the existing TIF but applies to all future large-scale incentive districts; business groups have filed a legal challenge that could invalidate the result.

name: Brown County

actions.title: Data Center Moratorium Proposal Declined by County Board
actions.summary: Brown County's planning committee declined to pursue a data center moratorium or any resolution opposing data center development, citing the county's lack of zoning jurisdiction over most municipalities and constraints under Wisconsin state law.

contextBlurb: A Brown County supervisor requested a pause on all data center activity pending state legislation, but the committee determined the county lacked zoning authority to act and that state law further complicated any formal moratorium. Community members, including a Green Bay School Board member, publicly criticized the county for what they characterized as an abdication of authority. Residents in the Village of Wrightstown, facing Cloverleaf Infrastructure's interest in a nearly 1-gigawatt AI data center, have continued to press their Village Board for a separate local moratorium.

name: City of Superior (Douglas County)

actions.title: One-Year Data Center Moratorium Resolution
actions.summary: The Superior City Council unanimously approved a one-year moratorium on data centers, citing the absence of any zoning definition for data centers and concern that nearby communities were being blindsided by large-scale proposals.

contextBlurb: Superior acted proactively as a nearby Duluth suburb weighed a massive Google data center proposal, and developer Cloverleaf Infrastructure expressed interest in northeast Wisconsin. Council member Garner Moffat brought the resolution forward, noting the city lacked any definition distinguishing small from large data centers in its zoning regulations. Superior became one of a growing list of Wisconsin communities—alongside Madison, Manitowoc County, Cassville, and Wrightstown—passing moratoriums within a short span.

name: City of Janesville (Rock County)

actions.title: Voter Ballot Initiative on Data Center Approval Threshold (Scheduled November 2026)
actions.summary: A ballot initiative is set for the November 2026 election in Janesville that would require voter approval for data center projects exceeding $450 million, modeled on Port Washington's April 2026 referendum and directed at a proposed $8 billion data center on the former GM plant site.

contextBlurb: Janesville faces at least three separate data center proposals totaling more than $9 billion in investment and over 1 gigawatt of power demand, including an $8 billion 'Viridian' project on the former General Motors brownfield site. Community pressure following Port Washington's pioneering April 2026 referendum has driven a similar ballot initiative onto Janesville's November 2026 ballot, which would require voter sign-off on projects above $450 million. The Wisconsin PSC approved an Alliant Energy–Meta power deal in May 2026 for a related Dodge County project but criticized the opaque rate structure.
